title: Bowling for Columbine
full_review:
"Bowling for Columbine" (United Artists), by 1989's "Roger & Me" filmmaker Michael Moore, uses guerrilla video journalism techniques to ridicule and blame the National Rifle Association and an American mindset for the Columbine High School massacre in Colorado and for random acts of violence throughout the United States.

One teacher and 12 students, including the suicidal shooters, died in the Columbine tragedy April 20,1999. Later it was learned the shooters had bowled earlier in the morning.

Moore, who writes, produces, directs and acts as sole interviewer in his movies, uses the incident as the keystone for his thesis that the NRA, its members and its president, Charlton Heston, are culpable for such shootings.

Although Moore is sympathetic to many of the people he interviews, he ambushes others, such as hunters and gun collectors, who are often too inarticulate to defend themselves and too guileless to see how he'll ridicule them through his selection of questions and responses. His questions frequently are loaded to defy a coherent response from the unprepared.

His most disingenuous encounter, perhaps, is with Heston, who is shown twice in earlier clips uttering his much-quoted "from my cold, dead hands" line at NRA rallies. But when, in his home, the older and somewhat frail Heston is provoked by the agenda-driven Moore, the actor shakes his guest's hand and retreats from camera range.

TV mogul and onetime "American Bandstand" host Dick Clark, whom Moore tries to corner for employing welfare-to-work moms at a club-restaurant, tells aides to close his car door and drive off.

Moore is more affable with a couple of other celebrities: rock star Marilyn Manson, whom some blamed for his influence on the Columbine shooters, and Matt Stone, an irreverent Columbine alumni who went on to co-create the TV series "South Park."

Among those who look particularly foolish are a young man who boasts he has made a bomb the size of a tennis ball. Another is James Nichols, brother of Oklahoma City bombing co-conspirator Terry Nichols.

Moore constructs a valid inquiry into the nature and frequency of American violence and the ease with which weapons and ammunition may be obtained, but he clouds his case with an assortment of specious arguments. He tries to ascribe the Columbine tragedy, for example, to the school's proximity to Lockheed Martin, which manufactures missiles.

Slipping off onto one of several tangents, Moore includes a short, primitive, racially charged cartoon that attempts to connect the dots from the importation of slaves from Africa to the oppression of blacks in America today. He also blames the country's violence on American foreign policy, which is dumped into a montage of news banners that collectively distort a half-century of U.S. involvement abroad. Frequent news coverage of violence is also responsible, he maintains, for encouraging Americans to fear that they need to be armed.

"Bowling for Columbine" may encourage enlightened dialogue on some of its notions. The danger is that it may be accepted too much at face value by impressionable audiences unaware of the manipulation built into Moore's arguments.

Due to recurring rough language and some intense images in video and newsreel clips, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
